title: Cold vs. Flu: Differences, Self-Care, and When to Seek Help
content:
The common cold and influenza (flu) are both respiratory illnesses caused by viruses, but they are caused by different virus families and differ in severity and onset.

Colds (caused by rhinoviruses and others) typically develop gradually. Symptoms centre on the upper respiratory tract: runny or stuffy nose, sore throat, sneezing, and mild cough. Fever is uncommon in adults with colds. Most colds resolve within 7–10 days.

Influenza (caused by influenza A and B viruses) typically comes on suddenly. Symptoms include high fever (38–40 degrees Celsius / 100–104 degrees Fahrenheit), severe muscle aches and fatigue, headache, and dry cough. Nasal symptoms are less prominent than with a cold. Flu can lead to serious complications — including pneumonia — particularly in adults over 65, children under 5, pregnant women, and people with chronic health conditions.

Self-care for both illnesses:
Rest allows the immune system to focus on fighting the infection. Staying home reduces spread to others.
Fluids are important to prevent dehydration, especially if fever is present. Warm broth, water, and herbal tea can help soothe symptoms.
Over-the-counter symptom relief: paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen for fever and aches; decongestants and antihistamines for nasal symptoms. Follow package dosing instructions.
Never give aspirin to children or teenagers with viral illness due to the risk of Reye's syndrome.

Antibiotics do not treat colds or flu — both are viral. Unnecessary antibiotic use contributes to antibiotic resistance.

Antiviral medications (such as oseltamivir / Tamiflu) are available for influenza and work best when started within 48 hours of symptom onset. They require a prescription and are most beneficial for high-risk individuals.

Seek medical attention if you experience: difficulty breathing or shortness of breath; persistent chest pain or pressure; confusion or altered consciousness; severe or persistent vomiting; symptoms that improve and then worsen again (which can indicate a secondary bacterial infection).

Flu vaccination every year is the most effective way to prevent influenza. The vaccine is updated annually to match circulating strains and is recommended for everyone aged 6 months and older.
